questions.stem: After executing a `lookup_order` call, the developer's loop sends the next request with only the model's previous assistant message appended. The model then calls `lookup_order` again with identical arguments, sometimes four or five times, before giving up. What is wrong?

options.text: The loop never appends a `tool_result` block with the matching `tool_use_id`, so the model never sees the output.
options.why: Tool results must go back into history, or the model keeps asking.

options.text: `lookup_order` lacks an idempotency key, so the model can't tell that its earlier call has already completed.
options.why: Idempotency protects side effects. It doesn't deliver results to the model.

options.text: The model needs `tool_choice` set to `none` after the first call, which stops it from requesting the same tool again.
options.why: This blocks all further tool use instead of supplying the missing result.

options.text: The system prompt should forbid repeating a tool call with identical arguments within one conversation.
options.why: This treats the symptom. The model repeats the call because it never got the result.

questions.explanation: An agentic loop runs the tools, appends `tool_result` blocks, and calls the model again. Missing results cause repeated calls.

questions.stem: Larkspur's support playbook lists five rules. A recent incident review found that the agent broke each of them at least once, at rates between 0.5% and 3%. The engineering team has capacity to build programmatic enforcement for only two of them this quarter, and will handle the rest through prompting and monitoring. Which TWO rules should get programmatic enforcement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: No refund may be processed until `get_customer` has returned a verified identity for the customer.
options.why: This is a compliance rule with financial and privacy consequences, so it must hold every time.

options.text: Refunds above $500 require explicit approval from a human on the Tier-2 team before they are issued.
options.why: This is a financial control, so it must be deterministic.

options.text: Offer the loyalty programme to customers who have placed three or more orders in the past twelve months.
options.why: A miss here costs little, so prompt-level guidance is enough.

options.text: Never share internal warehouse codes or system names in customer-facing replies, even if the customer asks.
options.why: This is a real concern, but leaking a code is low-impact compared with an unauthorised refund. Prompts and output filters handle it well enough.

options.text: Apologise once, not repeatedly, when an order is delayed by more than five business days.
options.why: This is a matter of conversational tone, which prompts handle well.

questions.explanation: With limited capacity, put code-level enforcement on the rules where a single violation has compliance or financial consequences.

questions.stem: A PreToolUse hook now blocks `process_refund` for unverified customers. In testing, after a blocked call the agent either retried the same refund in a loop, or told the customer the refund had been issued. The hook currently returns an empty result when it blocks. What should the hook return instead?

options.text: A structured denial such as "blocked: customer not verified, call get_customer first", so the agent knows what to do next.
options.why: An informative denial lets the agent recover correctly.

options.text: A success response carrying a hidden `pending_review` flag, so the customer gets a smooth experience while the refund waits.
options.why: Masking a block as success caused the false "refund issued" message seen in testing.

options.text: An exception that ends the session and opens a security ticket for every blocked refund attempt.
options.why: This is disproportionate for an ordering mistake the agent can recover from.

options.text: The same empty result, plus a system-prompt note explaining that an empty refund result means verification is required.
options.why: This is indirect and probabilistic. Put the reason in the tool result itself.

questions.explanation: Hooks should block deterministically and explain why. The reason in the result is what drives a correct recovery.

questions.stem: After two compliance incidents, a director proposes replacing the agent with a fixed decision tree: if the message mentions "refund", ask for the order ID, then look it up, then refund. Data shows that 38% of refund chats also raise a second topic (shipping, sizing or account changes), and many customers phrase refund requests without the word "refund". What is the best response to the proposal?

options.text: Adopt the tree for all refund conversations, since determinism is exactly what the compliance incidents call for.
options.why: This addresses compliance, but rigid trees fail the 38% multi-topic chats and the varied phrasings.

options.text: Keep the agentic loop for conversation flow, and add code-level gates for the compliance rules that failed.
options.why: Model-driven flow plus programmatic guardrails is the intended hybrid design.

options.text: Keep the agent unchanged, and add stronger compliance instructions with examples drawn from the two incidents.
options.why: Prompt-only fixes leave compliance probabilistic.

options.text: Use the tree for chats containing "refund" and the agent for everything else, so each handles what it does best.
options.why: Keyword routing misses many refund requests and splits the multi-topic chats.

questions.explanation: Let the model drive the conversation, and let code enforce the rules that can't be broken.

questions.stem: In about 5% of order-status questions, the agent answers from earlier conversation context instead of calling `lookup_order`, and sometimes reports a stale status. A developer proposes setting `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` on every request. What should you expect, and what is the better fix?

options.text: `any` forces `lookup_order` specifically, so stale answers stop. The cost is a little extra latency on each turn.
options.why: `any` forces some tool, not a specific one. Forcing one named tool requires the named-tool form.

options.text: `any` only forces a tool when one is relevant, so it is safe. Combine it with a prompt telling the agent to refresh order statuses.
options.why: This describes `auto`, not `any`.

options.text: The agent could never reply in plain text. Better: say in the tool description and prompt that order status must always be fetched fresh.
options.why: `any` forces a tool call on every turn. Improving the guidance targets the actual gap.

options.text: `any` disables parallel tool calls, which slows multi-lookup conversations. Use `auto` and accept the occasional stale answer.
options.why: That isn't what `any` does, and accepting stale answers ignores the problem.

questions.explanation: `auto` lets the model decide, `any` forces some tool on every turn, and a named tool forces that tool. Forcing tool use globally breaks normal replies.

questions.stem: A customer wants a refund on a custom-engraved watch ($310, delivered 10 days ago) because the engraving has a typo. The refund policy covers damaged, defective and late items, but doesn't mention personalised goods. Two similar cases last month were resolved differently by different human agents. What should the agent do?

options.text: Treat the typo as a defect, since an engraving error is arguably a manufacturing fault, and refund within policy.
options.why: This is a plausible interpretation, but the agent would be inventing policy, and humans have already disagreed on these cases.

options.text: Treat it as a policy gap: tell the customer the case needs review, and escalate with a structured summary.
options.why: Policy gaps are escalation triggers, especially when even humans decide them inconsistently.

options.text: Ask for a photo of the engraving, and refund if it shows a clear error, since that is objective evidence of a defect.
options.why: Gathering evidence is useful, but the decision still has no policy basis.

options.text: Decline politely, since personalised goods aren't listed as eligible, and offer a 15% discount on a replacement.
options.why: This also improvises policy, in the opposite direction.

questions.explanation: Escalate cases the policy doesn't cover. The inconsistent human decisions are a signal that the policy needs a decision-maker.

questions.stem: For an EV-charging brief, the coordinator assigned one search subagent "EV charging pricing" and another "EV charging business models". The two runs returned 31 sources between them, 19 of which appeared in both, and used about 40% more search budget than planned. What should the coordinator do differently?

options.text: Partition scope explicitly when delegating: give each subagent distinct boundaries and exclusions, so their work doesn't overlap.
options.why: Explicit partitioning prevents duplicated work.

options.text: Let both run as now, and have the synthesis agent deduplicate the overlapping sources and findings before writing.
options.why: The budget has already been spent by then. This treats the symptom.

options.text: Merge the two subtopics into a single search task, so one subagent covers both without repeating any searches.
options.why: This loses parallelism and focus on two genuinely different questions.

options.text: Share a cache of fetched URLs between subagents, so the second one skips any source the first has already read.
options.why: This saves fetches, but both subagents still pursue overlapping questions, and their findings will duplicate.

questions.explanation: The coordinator owns decomposition, including clear, non-overlapping scopes.

questions.stem: Client feedback scores show that 30% of briefs have at least one section that is thin, typically one paragraph with a single source. Other sections are rich. The coordinator currently delegates once per section and passes everything straight to synthesis. The total cost per brief may rise by at most 15%. Thin sections are spread unevenly: some briefs have none, others have two or three. Which change best improves completeness within that budget?

options.text: Run every section's subagent twice with different prompts, and merge both outputs to increase coverage.
options.why: This roughly doubles the cost, far over the 15% budget, and isn't targeted.

options.text: Have the report agent expand thin sections using general background knowledge, clearly labelled as context.
options.why: Unsourced padding violates the citation requirement.

options.text: Add a refinement loop: the coordinator checks each section against the quality criteria and re-delegates only for gaps.
options.why: Targeted follow-up spends budget only where sections are thin.

options.text: Raise every search subagent's result limit by 50%, so each section starts with more raw material.
options.why: This spends budget on sections that were already rich.

questions.explanation: Coordinators can run iterative refinement: evaluate the output against criteria, then re-delegate targeted follow-ups.

questions.stem: The team wants a reusable fact-checker the coordinator can call for any brief. It needs its own instructions, only fetch access (no search), and a clear description so the coordinator knows when to use it. It must not see the coordinator's accumulated context. How should it be defined in the Agent SDK?

options.text: As a section of the coordinator's system prompt that tells it to adopt a strict fact-checker role when verifying claims.
options.why: This gives no context isolation and no tool restriction, so both stated requirements fail.

options.text: As an `AgentDefinition` with a description, a system prompt and a restricted tools list, invoked through Task.
options.why: This meets every stated requirement: separate instructions, restricted tools, isolated context and a description for selection.

options.text: As an MCP server exposing a `fact_check` tool that internally calls the model with fetch access.
options.why: This is workable but heavyweight, and it moves agent logic into tool infrastructure.

options.text: As a project skill with `allowed-tools: WebFetch` in its SKILL.md frontmatter, loaded by the coordinator when needed.
options.why: Skills are Claude Code assets, not the SDK's mechanism for defining subagents.

questions.explanation: `AgentDefinition` is the SDK construct for specialised subagents with their own prompt, tools and isolated context.

questions.stem: A client orders a monthly brief with a fixed structure: market size, top five players, regulatory changes and a 12-month outlook. The sources are mostly the same each month. The client values consistency between months and wants each section validated before the brief is assembled. Which workflow design fits best?

options.text: Fully adaptive decomposition each month, so the coordinator can find angles the fixed structure would miss.
options.why: Adaptive decomposition adds month-to-month variability that the client explicitly doesn't want.

options.text: A single comprehensive prompt that writes the whole brief from the source set, since the structure is familiar.
options.why: This loses the per-section validation the client asked for.

options.text: Reuse last month's brief, and ask the report agent to update only the figures it detects as having changed.
options.why: This risks carrying stale claims forward and missing new developments.

options.text: A prompt chain with a stage per section and validation between stages, since the structure is stable.
options.why: Chaining suits predictable structures and gives natural points for validation.

questions.explanation: Use fixed chaining for known, repeatable structures and adaptive decomposition for open-ended discovery.

questions.stem: The synthesis agent receives prose summaries from subagents. In an audit of 20 briefs, 17% of quantitative claims couldn't be traced to the document or page they came from, and several were attributed to the wrong year. Which TWO changes to the subagents' outputs help most? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Return findings as structured records: claim, evidence excerpt, source ID or URL, and page or section.
options.why: Structured records keep attribution intact as findings pass between agents.

options.text: Attach metadata such as publication date and source type (regulator, analyst or press) to each finding.
options.why: Dates fix the wrong-year attributions, and source type supports credibility judgements.

options.text: Return longer, more detailed prose summaries, so more context about each source survives into synthesis.
options.why: More prose doesn't make attribution traceable.

options.text: Have subagents write their sections directly into the final report, so citations never pass through synthesis.
options.why: This bypasses synthesis and the coordinator, and fragments the report.

options.text: Add a final pass in which the report agent re-searches the web for a source for each statistic in the brief.
options.why: Retrofitting citations is unreliable and can attach the wrong source.

questions.explanation: Pass structured content plus metadata between agents to preserve provenance.

questions.stem: On large briefs, the coordinator's context grows past 150k tokens, because each subagent returns the full text of every page it fetched (about 8k tokens a page). In the later steps of these briefs, the coordinator re-assigns work that is already done and loses track of which sections are complete. What is the best fix?

options.text: Move the coordinator to a model with a larger context window, so all the fetched content fits without truncation.
options.why: Attention still dilutes over the extra content, and the cost grows.

options.text: Have the coordinator summarise each subagent's output as it arrives, keeping only its own summaries in history.
options.why: Better, but the raw pages still pass through the coordinator's context first.

options.text: Have subagents return concise structured findings with source references, not raw pages.
options.why: Subagents should absorb the verbose work and return only distilled results.

options.text: Cap each subagent at two fetched pages, so the coordinator receives at most about 16k tokens per subtask.
options.why: This limits bloat but cripples research depth.

questions.explanation: Keep the coordinator lean: subagents return structured summaries with metadata, not raw dumps.

questions.stem: `web_fetch` returns HTTP 403 for paywalled news sites. The tool currently reports this as a generic failure. Logs show the search subagent retrying paywalled URLs up to five times each, which wastes about 12% of fetch calls, before it moves on. How should the tool report this condition?

options.text: As a permission/access error with `isRetryable: false`, so the agent moves straight to alternative sources.
options.why: A categorised, non-retryable error stops futile retries immediately.

options.text: As an empty page with a success status, so the agent concludes there is nothing useful at that URL and moves on.
options.why: This stops the retries, but it disguises an access failure as an empty result.

options.text: As a transient error with a 60-second backoff hint, in case the paywall was a temporary glitch on the publisher's side.
options.why: This is the wrong category for a permanent condition, and it still wastes calls.

options.text: As a generic failure, but with a system-prompt rule telling the subagent not to retry any URL more than once.
options.why: This helps, but every 403 still costs one wasted retry, and the agent can't explain the gap.

questions.explanation: Error categories plus retryability let agents retry only transient failures.
